front_blocks.md: Define **indicator**.

back_blocks.md: An **indicator** is a substance that changes colour depending on whether a solution is **acidic** or **alkaline**, used to distinguish between the two.

cards.back_md: An **indicator** is a substance that changes colour depending on whether a solution is **acidic** or **alkaline**, used to distinguish between the two.

front_blocks.md: What colours does phenolphthalein show in acid and in alkali?

back_blocks.md: **Phenolphthalein** is **colourless** in acid and **pink** in alkali.

front_blocks.md: Litmus turns **..........** in acid and **..........** in alkali.

back_blocks.md: Litmus turns **red** in acid and **blue** in alkali.

cards.front_md: Litmus turns **..........** in acid and **..........** in alkali.
cards.back_md: Litmus turns **red** in acid and **blue** in alkali.

front_blocks.md: Why is universal indicator not suitable for titrations?

back_blocks.md: A **sharp colour change** is required to identify the titration **endpoint**. Universal indicator changes colour gradually across a range of pH values and cannot give a precise endpoint.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Litmus is a suitable indicator for acid-alkali titrations.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

**Litmus** is not suitable for titrations because its colour change is not sharp and it passes through a purple transition colour near neutral pH, making it difficult to identify the **endpoint** accurately.

front_blocks.md: On the pH scale, solutions with a pH of 0–3 are classified as **..........**,  pH 4–6 as **..........**,  pH 7 as **..........**,  pH 8–10 as **..........** and pH 11–14 as **..........** .

back_blocks.md: On the pH scale, solutions with a pH of 0–3 are classified as **strongly acidic**, pH 4–6 as **slightly acidic**, pH 7 as **neutral**, pH 8–10 as **slightly alkaline** and pH 11–14 as **strongly alkaline**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Universal indicator can be used to find the exact pH of a solution.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
**Universal indicator** gives only an **approximate** pH value. It cannot provide an exact reading because it shows a gradual range of colours rather than a sharp change.

front_blocks.md: How is universal indicator used to estimate the pH of a solution?

back_blocks.md: A few drops of **universal indicator** are added to the solution. The resulting colour is matched against a **colour chart** to give an approximate **pH** value.

front_blocks.md: Define **acid** (in aqueous solution).

back_blocks.md: An **acid** is a substance that, when dissolved in water, is a source of **hydrogen ions** (H<sup>+</sup>).

cards.back_md: An **acid** is a substance that, when dissolved in water, is a source of **hydrogen ions** (H<sup>+</sup>).

front_blocks.md: Define **alkali** (in aqueous solution).

back_blocks.md: An **alkali** is a substance that, when dissolved in water, is a source of **hydroxide ions** (OH<sup>-</sup>).

cards.back_md: An **alkali** is a substance that, when dissolved in water, is a source of **hydroxide ions** (OH<sup>-</sup>).

front_blocks.md: Acids in aqueous solution produce **..........** ions and alkalis in aqueous solution produce **..........** ions.

back_blocks.md: Acids in aqueous solution produce **H**<sup>**+**</sup> ions and alkalis in aqueous solution produce **OH**<sup>**-**</sup> ions.

cards.front_md: Acids in aqueous solution produce **..........** ions and alkalis in aqueous solution produce **..........** ions.
cards.back_md: Acids in aqueous solution produce **H**<sup>**+**</sup> ions and alkalis in aqueous solution produce **OH**<sup>**-**</sup> ions.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
All reactions of acids with other substances are neutralisation reactions.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

Neutralisation requires both a **salt** and **water** to be produced. When a **metal** reacts with an **acid**, a salt and **hydrogen gas** are formed — but no water — so it is not a neutralisation reaction.

front_blocks.md: What is the net ionic equation for all acid-base neutralisation reactions?

back_blocks.md: H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + OH<sup>-</sup> (aq) → H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
The **H**<sup>**+**</sup> ions from the acid react with the **OH**<sup>**-**</sup> ions from the alkali to produce **water**.

front_blocks.md: Why are bases added to soil to treat acidity?

back_blocks.md: Bases such as **limestone** and **quicklime** neutralise excess **acid** in the soil, raising the **pH** to a level at which crops can grow.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The pH of a neutral solution at room temperature is 7.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
A **neutral** solution has a pH of **7**. This corresponds to equal concentrations of **H**<sup>**+**</sup> and **OH**<sup>**-**</sup> ions in solution.

front_blocks.md: What are the products of the neutralisation of hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide?

back_blocks.md: **Sodium chloride** (NaCl) and **water** (H<sub>2</sub>O) are produced when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide solution.
